L000089	\begin{abstract}
L000090		Gravitational waves (GWs) in the $0.01\sim1$ Hz band encode unique signatures
L000091	of the early universe and merging compact objects, but they are beyond the
L000092	reach of existing observatories.  Theoretical models suggest that the Moon
L000093	could act as a resonant detector, but the unknown influence of its rugged surface and heterogeneous interior poses a challenge to the accurate modeling of its response.  Here, we
L000094	address this long-standing uncertainty by constructing the first
L000095	high-resolution, two-dimensional model of the lunar GW response, more realistic
L000096	than previous ones. We
L000097	achieve this by combining high-fidelity spectral-element
L000098	simulations with
L000099	the analytical power of normal-mode perturbation theory, thereby resolving
L000100	topographical effects down to 2 km grid spacing while maintaining the capacity
L000101	to discern global free-oscillation patterns.
L000102	This dual-methodology approach not only recovers the expected predominant quadrupole
L000103	($l=2$) oscillation mode, but also exposes a systematic signal amplification in thick-crust
L000104	regions.
L000105	This enhancement is traced by our normal-mode analysis to a mode-coupling process, in which the original quadrupolar oscillation induced by the passing GW distributes energy into a series of higher-order modes, the hybridized eigenmodes of a laterally heterogeneous Moon.
L000106	In certain narrow frequency ranges, we observe up to tenfold amplification spanning into the deci-hertz band, highlighting
L000107	the power of numerical simulations in resolving these structurally fine-tuned features for designing future detectors.
L000108	Our work establishes the Moon as a resonant GW detector albeit its complex topographical structures, and the resulting
L000109		amplification maps provide quantitative guide for the optimal landing site selection.
L000110	\end{abstract}

L000114	
L000115	
L000116	
L000117	\textit{Introduction.}---Gravitational waves (GWs) have been observed in the
L000118	hundred-hertz band by ground-based interferometers \cite{2016PhRvL.116f1102A,
L000119	1992Sci...256..325A, 2015CQGra..32b4001A, 2019NatAs...3...35K} and in the
L000120	nano-hertz band by pulsar timing arrays \cite{2023RAA....23g5024X,
L000121	2023A&A...678A..50E, 2023ApJ...951L...9A, 2023ApJ...951L...6R}. In between lies
L000122	the mid band ($0.01\sim1$ Hz) where many intriguing sources exist, including
L000123	the seeds of supermassive black holes, inspiraling binary stellar black holes
L000124	or neutron stars, supernovae, as well as quantum fluctuations in the early
L000125	universe \cite{2020CQGra..37u5011A,2024arXiv240207571C}.  The detection of
L000126	these sources defines the core science cases for future space-based GW
L000127	detectors like LISA, TianQin, Taiji \cite{2024arXiv240207571C,
L000128	2016CQGra..33c5010L, 2021PTEP.2021eA108L}, and other projects \cite{2011CQGra..28i4011K,2022IJMPD..3150039N}.
L000129	
L000130	An alternative proposal of detecting mid-band GWs is to find a celestial body
L000131	which can act as a giant resonant detector \cite{1960PhRv..117..306W,
L000132	1968PhT....21d..34W,1969ApJ...156..529D}. In this spirit, the Moon offers a
L000133	unique platform due to its quietness compared to the Earth
L000134	\cite{2009JGRE..11412003L}. Assuming spherical symmetry,  earlier analytical
L000135	works established that only the Moon's quadrupole ($l=2$) mode resonates with
L000136	GW \cite{1983NCimC...6...49B,1996CQGra..13.2865B}, and the resonant peaks lie
L000137	in the mid band \cite{1983NCimC...6...49B, 2019PhRvD.100d4048M,
L000138	PhysRevD.109.064092,2025PhRvD.111d4061M}. These one‑dimension models also revealed the
L000139	importance of lunar radial structure in determining the resonant frequencies
L000140	\cite{2024PhRvD.110f4025B,2025PhRvD.111d4061M}.
L000141	
L000142	In reality, the Moon is {\it not} a spherically symmetric body but has strong variations in both topography and crustal thickness, since altimetric surveys indicate tens of kilometers in topographic relief \cite{2010GeoRL..3718204S,2013Sci...339..671W} and lunar
L000143	gravity measurements reveal strong lateral variations in crustal thickness \cite{huang2022bombardment,
L000144	wieczorek1998potential}. Many studies based on
L000145	normal-mode perturbation theory \cite{1980GeoJ...61..261W,
L000146	1999tgs..book.....D} show that strong lateral velocity variations would severely impact the resonance of seismic wave propagation within the Earth, especially for the normal mode coupling and energy
L000147	redistribution \cite{1978GeoJ...53..335W,1983JGR....8810285M,2001GeoJI.146..833D}. However, the effect of such heterogeneity on the GW response of the Earth and the Moon remains unknown.
L000148	If not
L000149	properly understood, it may mislead our conclusion for lunar GW detection \cite{Chen2026-be}. This
L000150	issue is becoming even more pressing for the proposed projects like Lunar Gravitational-Wave Antenna (LGWA) \cite{2021ApJ...910....1H,
L000151	2023SSRv..219...67B}, Laser Interferometer Lunar Antenna (LILA) \cite{2025arXiv250811631J}, and other lunar GW projects \cite{2009AdSpR..43..167P,2021CQGra..38l5008A,2023SCPMA..6609513L}.
L000152	
L000153	Using conventional normal‑mode perturbation analysis \cite{1980GeoJ...61..261W,
L000154	1999tgs..book.....D} to address this issue presents distinct advantages and
L000155	limitations. A major advantage arises from the simplicity of the GW source
L000156	term: unlike earthquakes or moonquakes, which excite a broad spectrum of
L000157	seismic modes, GWs interact almost exclusively with the Moon’s quadrupole
L000158	($l=2$) modes, drastically simplifying the analytical description. However,
L000159	this approach becomes computationally demanding when accounting for the full
L000160	mode‑mixing induced by the lateral heterogeneity, and it struggles to provide a
L000161	fine‑scale description of the resulting surface displacement field.  To
L000162	complement the perturbation analysis, in the past few years we have developed
L000163	high‑fidelity numerical simulations based on the high-order finite-element method
L000164	(FEM), specifically the spectral‑element method (SEM)
L000165	\cite{2025PhRvD.111f3014Z,2026PhRvD.113b3031Z},
L000166	which enables precise modeling of wave propagation across realistic lunar
L000167	topography \cite{komatitsch2005spectral,
L000168	zhang2020procedure,2026PhRvD.113b3031Z}. Although computationally intensive,
L000169	the SEM provides a direct numerical testbed for verifying key analytical
L000170	predictions, particularly in regions of strong topographic and crustal
L000171	variations. However, three‑dimensional (3D) simulations remain computationally prohibitive for
L000172	long-duration GW signals. Therefore, it is essential to develop a novel
L000173	calculation framework that combines the high resolution of the FEM and the
L000174	generality of the normal-mode analysis
L000175	to reveal both the fine details of the lunar response and the underlying physical mechanism.
L000176	
L000177	For the above reason, we present the first structurally realistic model of the lunar GW response: high-precision two‑dimensional (2D) SEM simulations employed to resolve the effects of rugged topography and strong non-uniform crustal structures, while a 3D mode-coupling approach characterizes the global low-order response. Our results show that the Moon’s
L000178	crustal asymmetry acts as a potent amplifier, efficiently redistributing energy
L000179	from the GW‑excited quadrupole modes into a rich spectrum of higher‑order
L000180	spheroidal modes. This mode‑mixing process not only enhances signal
L000181	detectability in specific frequency bands but also indicates the potential of GW‑induced seismic responses to constrain the Moon’s 3D internal structure.
L000182

The black line indicates the great circle passing through Mare Humboldtianum, Mare Imbrium, and the SPA basin. The potential landing sites of Chang’e-7 and FFS are marked as stars around the south pole. (b) Crustal thickness model truncated at $l=4$. Solid lines represent crustal thickness contours in km. (c) The surface topography and crustal thickness along the great circle shown in (a). The outer black curve is the surface topography, exaggerated by a factor of 30 for visibility, and the inner black curve marks the crust bottom, whose radial position is drawn by exaggerating the crustal thickness by a factor of 5 inward from the surface, both relative to the mean lunar radius. The color fill encodes the local crustal thickness, highlighting its pronounced lateral variations. }
L000188	    \label{fig:fig1}

L000192	\textit{Numerical simulation of lunar response to GWs.}---We first perform 2D
L000193	numerical simulations to quantify how lunar topography and crustal structure
L000194	modulate the GW‑induced surface displacement and velocity fields. Details of modeling and parameter setting can
L000195	be found in Supplemental Material \cite{supplemental}. Our lunar
L000196	model integrates topographic and crustal-thickness data from the LOLA
L000197	\cite{2010GeoRL..3718204S} and GRAIL \cite{2013Sci...339..671W} missions,
L000198	incorporating major structural features such as the South Pole–Aitken (SPA)
L000199	basin, Mare Imbrium, and Mare Humboldtianum (Figure~\ref{fig:fig1}). To reduce the extremely heavy computational cost, we
L000200	extract a typical 2D profile along a selected great circle of the real 3D model. Dyson-type force density is applied to model
L000201	the GW sources \cite{1969ApJ...156..529D}. To accurately capture short-wavelength
L000202	scattering in the deci-hertz regime, this simulation utilizes a high-resolution
L000203	topographic model with a grid spacing of approximately 2.0 km. Our model achieves a maximum
L000204	resolved frequency of 0.36 Hz with a time step constrained to $5\times 10^{-3}$ s, ensuring
L000205	both numerical stability and computational tractability. Then we use the SEM
L000206	\cite{2025PhRvD.111f3014Z} to simulate the excitation of seismic activity by
L000207	GWs, employing a broadband source time function centered near $0.1$ Hz. We focus on the response in the
L000208	frequency band up to $0.2$~Hz. Figure~\ref{fig:fig2}(a--d) shows
L000209	that the lateral heterogeneity of structures has significant impact on the
L000210	lunar response to GWs. Compared with the results obtained by spherically
L000211	layered models \cite{PhysRevD.109.064092, 2025PhRvD.111f3014Z}, the wavefronts
L000212	in the realistic model are evidently distorted, especially in Mare Imbrium, Mare
L000213	Humboldtianum, and the SPA basin.
L000214	
L000215	To quantify the impact of lunar topography and crustal thickness variation, we define an
L000216	amplification ratio $M_E$ as the ratio of local displacement energy ($|\bm{\vec{s}}(\vec{r}, \omega)|^2$) \footnote{Note that $\omega=2\pi f$. The frequency units ``mHz'' or ``Hz'' in this work refer to
L000217	$f$ rather than the angular frequency $\omega$.}
L000218	with or without lateral heterogeneity (marked with ``P'' or ``NP''), integrated over frequency:
L000219	
L000220	\begin{eqnarray}
L000221	\label{eq:magnification}
L000222	M_E(\vec{r}) & = & \frac{ \int_{\omega_{\text{min}}}^{\omega_{\text{max}}} \langle |\bm{\vec{s}}^{\text{P}}(\vec{r}, \omega)|^2 \rangle_{\text{pol}} \mathrm{d}\omega }{ \int_{\omega_{\text{min}}}^{\omega_{\text{max}}} \langle |\bm{\vec{s}}^{\text{NP}}(\vec{r}, \omega)|^2 \rangle_{\text{pol}} \mathrm{d}\omega } ~.
L000223	\end{eqnarray}
L000224	
L000225	Here, $\langle \rangle_{\text{pol}}$ denotes an average over all polarization, in order to
L000226	separate the amplification due to lunar structure from polarization-induced variations in the GW amplitude. More details of this equation are discussed in the Supplemental Material \cite{supplemental}.
L000227	
L000228	Figure~\ref{fig:fig2}e presents the distribution of $M_E$ along the typical great circle (integrated up to 0.2~Hz). The spatial characteristics generally show strong correlations
L000229	with both topography and crustal thickness. Notably, thick-crust regions
L000230	(e.g., highlands) show an average signal amplification (red curve in Figure~\ref{fig:fig2}e). However, in some places
L000231	such as Mare Imbrium, where the topography has almost no relief, the
L000232	amplification ratios still vary dramatically with the varying crustal
L000233	thickness. This key observation demonstrates that crustal thickness rather than
L000234	topography is the dominant factor of governing the amplification effect. Hence, we
L000235	should pay more attention to the crustal thickness when evaluating lunar local
L000236	response to GWs in future works.
L000237	
L000238	To find the optimal frequency band for GW search, we plot the
L000239	frequency-dependent amplification ratio $m_E (f)$, defined as
L000240	
L000241	\begin{eqnarray}
L000242	\label{eq:freq-magnification}
L000243	m_E(\vec{r},f) & = & \frac{ \langle |\bm{\vec{s}}^{\text{P}}(\vec{r}, 2\pi f)|^2 \rangle_{\text{pol}}  }{  \langle |\bm{\vec{s}}^{\text{NP}}(\vec{r}, 2\pi f)|^2 \rangle_{\text{pol}}  } ~,
L000244	\end{eqnarray}
L000245	
L000246	in Figure~\ref{fig:fig2}f, where we have applied a median-filter smoothing to
L000247	reveal fundamental patterns. The plot shows that the structurally induced
L000248	signal enhancement is a broadband phenomenon. In the lower frequency regime
L000249	($\le 0.04$~Hz), the amplification exhibits rich spectral peaks with narrow
L000250	bandwidths [also see Figs.~(A3) and (A4) \cite{supplemental}]. These peak
L000251	frequencies align closely with the resonant frequencies of the lunar response
L000252	function \cite{2025PhRvD.111f3014Z}, suggesting a direct link to the normal
L000253	modes of the Moon. Crucially, near the optimal sensitivity band of proposed
L000254	lunar antennas (around $0.1$ Hz), this localized energy magnification
L000255	$m_{E}(f)$ not only persists but further intensifies. The broadband spatial
L000256	variations in this deci-hertz regime remain tightly correlated with the
L000257	thick-crust topography. For example, on the highlands surrounding the SPA basin
L000258	(between $\varphi=70^{\circ}$ and $120^{\circ}$), $m_E (f)$ can reach tenfold,
L000259	with peak amplifications often exceeding those observed at lower frequencies.

L000274	\textit{Normal mode perturbation method.}---The observed close correspondence
L000275	between crust thickness and GW signal amplification in our numerical
L000276	simulations can be understood in the theoretical framework of normal-mode
L000277	perturbation and mixing. In the ideal case where the Moon is spherically symmetric, non-rotating, elastic,
L000278	and isotropic (SNREI),
L000279	its free oscillation can be
L000280	described by a series of orthonormal normal modes $|k\rangle \equiv |\sigma, n, l, m\rangle$ which are eigenfunctions of the secular equation
L000281	
L000282	\begin{eqnarray}
L000283	\mathcal{V} |k\rangle = \omega_k^2 \mathcal{T}|k\rangle
L000284	\end{eqnarray}
L000285	
L000286	\cite{1999tgs..book.....D}.
L000287	Here, $\sigma = S/T$ indicates the mode type (Spheroidal or Toroidal), $n$ is the radial quantum number, and $(l,m)$ are the angular momentum quantum number and magnetic quantum number. $\mathcal{V}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ are potential and kinetic operators, respectively.
L000288	The presence of surface topography and crustal variation perturbs the operators by $\delta \mathcal{V}$ and $\delta \mathcal{T}$,
L000289	restructuring the eigenmodes. Given that the perturbation is small, the new modes can be approximated by a linear combination of the
L000290	basic SNREI modes, so that
L000291	
L000292	\begin{eqnarray}
L000293	\label{eq:hybridization}
L000294	|i\rangle & = & \sum_k C_{ki} |k\rangle~.
L000295	\end{eqnarray}
L000296	
L000297	For this reason, the new modes are also known as the ``hybridized modes''.
L000298	The transformation matrix $\mathbf{C}$ satisfies the perturbed equation
L000299	
L000300	\begin{eqnarray}
L000301	\label{eq:eigenproblem}
L000302	\sum_{k'} (\omega_k^2 \delta_{kk'} + V_{kk'}) C_{k'i} & = & \Omega_i^2 \sum_{k'} (\delta_{kk'} + T_{kk'}) C_{k'i} \label{eq:eig}
L000303	\end{eqnarray}
L000304	
L000305	\cite{2001GeoJI.146..833D}, where $\Omega_i$ denotes the perturbed
L000306	eigenfrequency, $V_{kk'} = \langle k | \delta\mathcal{V} | k' \rangle$ and
L000307	$T_{kk'} = \langle k | \delta\mathcal{T} | k' \rangle$ are the elements of the
L000308	coupling matrices which can be calculated using Woodhouse kernels
L000309	\cite{1980GeoJ...61..261W}.
L000310	
L000311	GWs exert a tidal force $\bm{\vec{f}}_{\text{GW}}$ on the Moon. Owing to their quadrupole character, this force
L000312	couples almost exclusively to the unperturbed $l=2$ modes.
L000313	In a laterally heterogeneous Moon, however, these unperturbed SNREI modes are no longer the true eigenmodes. Instead,
L000314	they hybridize according to Equation~(\ref{eq:hybridization}). Consequently, the energy initially in the
L000315	quadrupole modes is systematically redistributed into the hybridized mode spectrum.
L000316	Following the standard Green-function approach \cite{1983NCimC...6...49B,2019PhRvD.100d4048M} as well as perturbation formalism introduced above, this mode mixing process is captured by the following equation,
L000317	
L000318	\begin{eqnarray}
L000319	\label{eq:response}
L000320	\bm{\vec{s}}^{\text{P}}(\vec{r}, \omega) & = & \sum_i \frac{\langle \vec{r}|i\rangle \langle i | \bm{\vec{f}}_{\text{GW}} \rangle}{\Omega_i^2 - \omega^2} \nonumber \\& = &\sum_i \frac{\sum_{k}C_{ki}\bm{\vec{u}}_k(\vec{r})}{\Omega_i^2 - \omega^2} \left( \sum_{k' \in \{\sigma l=S2\}} C_{k'i}^* f_{k'} \right) ~,
L000321	\end{eqnarray}
L000322	
L000323	where $\bm{\vec{s}}^{\text{P}}(\vec{r}, \omega)$ is the seismic displacement
L000324	field at location $\vec{r}$, $\bm{\vec{u}}_k(\vec{r}) = \langle \vec{r}|k\rangle $ is the unperturbed
L000325	free-oscillation pattern, and $f_{k'}$ is the projection of the GW force
L000326	onto the unperturbed mode $|k'\rangle$. Other details of this core
L000327	equation can be found in the Supplemental Material C, D and F \cite{supplemental}.
L000328	
L000329	We implement this framework using the topography model derived from
L000330	NASA's GRAIL Model 2 data \cite{2013Sci...339..671W}, which is already visualized in
L000331	Fig.~\ref{fig:fig1}(a). For comparison, the one-dimension SNREI model is
L000332	adopted from our previous work with slight modifications \cite{webs}. To maintain computational tractability while preserving
L000333	key large-scale asymmetries, notably the farside–nearside dichotomy, we truncate
L000334	the spherical-harmonic expansion of the Moon at $l_{\rm max}=4$, yielding the
L000335	approximate lunar model shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:fig1}(b). In the hybridized mode
L000336	calculation, we allow free-oscillation modes up to  $l=6$ and $n=100$,
L000337	reflecting both the selection rule and numerical feasibility. Toroidal modes
L000338	are excluded because GWs couple predominantly to spheroidal modes, and toroidal
L000339	eigenfunctions exhibit lower accuracy in standard solvers such as MINEOS
L000340	\cite{mineos2011}. While computing resource limits this perturbation analysis to a relatively narrow frequency band under $\sim 0.02~$Hz \footnote{Mode-perturbation approach calculations are done within two hours on a personal desktop computer without a dedicated GPU, showing its advantage on narrow-band, low-frequency global (full-Moon) analysis.}, the physical mechanism of energy redistribution validated here provides the fundamental explanation for the broadband amplification observed in our deci-hertz numerical results.

L000348	
L000349	Fig.~\ref{fig:fig3}(a) shows the band-integrated total magnification
L000350	$M_E(\vec{r})$ across the lunar surface.  This map reveals a robust and
L000351	systematic pattern, with values deviating from unity by approximately
L000352	$10\%$, consistent with the crustal-thickness dependence observed in our 2D numerical simulations.  This spatial pattern exhibits a clear correlation with the underlying
L000353	crustal structure shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:fig1}(b): regions of thin crust, such
L000354	as the nearside maria, consistently exhibit de‑amplification ($M_E<1$), whereas
L000355	the thick‑crust terrains of the farside highlands show pronounced
L000356	amplification. This correlation confirms the role of crustal thickness in
L000357	modulating the Moon’s global seismic response to GWs. It also points to a
L000358	direct link between lateral heterogeneity and surface observables.
L000359	
L000360	To more clearly trace the cause of the amplification, Fig.~\ref{fig:fig3}(b)
L000361	isolates the contribution to $M_E$ from the fundamental quadrupole mode
L000362	$\bm{\vec{u}}_{l=2}$ alone.  The resulting map shows values near unity, with
L000363	much smaller variation ($\sim4\%$) and weaker correlation to crustal
L000364	thickness. This result implies that the amplification pattern seen in
L000365	Fig.~\ref{fig:fig3}(a) is not primarily due to modulation of the $l=2$ mode,
L000366	but rather emerges from the collective response of higher-order modes ($l>2$)
L000367	excited through mode mixing.
L000368	
L000369	\textit{Discussions and implications.}---In this Letter, we have elucidated how
L000370	the rugged surface and heterogeneous crust of the Moon can modulate the surface
L000371	seismic signals triggered by GWs. We achieve this by developing
L000372	a calculation framework which combines the advantages of
L000373	two complementary approaches: a perturbation theory provides an efficient and transparent
L000374	physical picture of global mode mixing, whereas the SEM delivers the high spatial
L000375	resolution required to capture complex local wave-field distortions at the
L000376	expense of greater computational cost.
L000377	
L000378	Our SEM simulation not only recovers the GW-induced quadrupole mode of the
L000379	lunar free oscillation but also reveals a close link of the seismic amplitude
L000380	to the crustal thickness. On average, the seismic signal can be amplified by
L000381	$10\%$ in thick-crust regions. In some narrow frequency ranges, the
L000382	amplification can even exceed one order of magnitude. Crucially, our
L000383	high-frequency simulations confirm that this strong amplification persists
L000384	around $0.1$ Hz, agreeing well with the optimal sensitivity window of
L000385	proposed lunar seismometer arrays.  These findings establish a direct link
L000386	between crustal structure and GW detectability. Regions characterized by
L000387	thicker crust, particularly the farside highlands, consistently exhibit an
L000388	amplification of the GW signal, therefore offer better opportunities for GW
L000389	detection. However, the relationship between topography and signal
L000390	amplification is highly complex and frequency-dependent. While broadband
L000391	integrated magnification correlates positively with crustal thickness, our
L000392	high-resolution simulations reveal that in certain narrow frequency bands
L000393	(e.g., around 0.06 Hz), local topography can induce strong focusing effects probably caused by trapped waves in basins,
L000394	leading to significant signal amplification even in regions with a relatively
L000395	thin crust. This structural complexity underscores the importance of our
L000396	2D/3D modeling in real application scenarios, such as LGWA or LILA. Optimal site
L000397	selection for seismometers cannot rely solely on macro-scale
L000398	crustal thickness; it requires mission-specific, high-resolution numerical
L000399	simulations tuned to the detectors' target sensitivity bands to fully exploit
L000400	these localized, frequency-dependent amplification zones.
L000401	
L000402	Our simulations also pinpoint the strongest signal amplification in a
L000403	couple of frequency bands that can be as narrow as $\sim0.1\ \mathrm{mHz}$ [Fig.~(A3) \cite{supplemental}]. Resolving such narrow features requires
L000404	long-duration, low-noise observations since a bandwidth of $0.1\ \mathrm{mHz}$
L000405	implies a minimum observational period of $T\sim 1/(0.1~{\rm
L000406	mHz})= 10^{4}\ \mathrm{s}\approx 2.8\ \mathrm{h}$. Therefore,
L000407	continuous seismic data collection spanning one day or longer is recommended.
L000408	
L000409	The correlation between signal amplification and crust thickness is also
L000410	verified by our analytical normal-mode perturbation model.  The analysis further
L000411	identifies mode mixing as the origin of the enhancement: the Moon's crustal
L000412	asymmetry reshapes its eigenmodes, enabling the energy from a purely
L000413	quadrupolar perturbation, such as that imposed by a passing GW, to transfer into
L000414	an ensemble of higher-order free-oscillation modes. Such a correlated,
L000415	structured signal across the lunar surface differs fundamentally from the
L000416	stochastic, spatially incoherent background of seismic noise. By employing a
L000417	spatial correlation approach (e.g., see Ref.~\cite{2024PhRvD.110d3009Y}) that incorporates
L000418	our theoretical model of the hybridized modes, we can in principle
L000419	statistically separate the GW-induced seismic response from the spectrally and
L000420	spatially diffuse lunar seismic background.
L000421	
L000422	
L000423	Several caveats are worth mentioning. Although computational costs restricted
L000424	our SEM simulations to 2D, previous 2D-vs-3D comparisons
L000425	\cite{zhang2022dichotomy} support the reliability of this approach.
L000426	Furthermore, despite differing dimensionalities, the 2D SEM and fully 3D
L000427	mode-coupling analysis yield consistent, crustal-thickness-dependent
L000428	amplification patterns at low frequencies (Figs.~\ref{fig:fig2} and
L000429	\ref{fig:fig3}). This agreement suggests the 2D great-circle model captures the
L000430	dominant GW response, since the $l=2$ driving force and leading hybridized
L000431	modes project strongly onto this plane, implying that 3D SEM simulations will
L000432	largely preserve these qualitative trends. Analytically, the mode-coupling
L000433	calculation excluded toroidal modes and was truncated at a relatively low
L000434	spherical harmonic degree. Furthermore, our current model does not resolve
L000435	the km- to sub-km-scale heterogeneity or the pervasive fracturing of the lunar
L000436	megaregolith \cite{ZhangX2022,Onodera2022,Wiggins2019}.  Including them may affect
L000437	the lunar response at the
L000438	the upper end of the deci-hertz band, where the seismic wavelength becomes comparable to
L000439	these small scatterers. In this regime, multiple scattering randomizes the
L000440	phase of the GW‑induced wavefield and, as a result, prolongs the seismic signal
L000441	\cite{Latham1970,Nakamura1983}.
L000442	
L000443	Future work should bridge these gaps by performing fully 3D SEM simulations and extending the mode-coupling basis to higher $l_{\max}$. Additionally, with finer topographical models and expanded computational resources, subsequent simulations could probe higher-frequency bands, where small-scale scattering and fracturing
L000444	are expected to enhance the spatial and spectral variability of the local response. Finally, while this study focuses on polarization-averaged global correlations, individual GW events may exhibit sharper local resonances due to constructive interference; modeling these complex, event-specific interactions will be crucial for precise source parameter estimation in future observations.
L000445	
L000446	Finally, we emphasize that the integration of global mode‑coupling theory with
L000447	high‑resolution SEM simulations provides the framework necessary to reach the target of calibrating
L000448	the Moon as a resonant GW antenna. Beyond enabling the detection of mid‑band GW
L000449	sources, this approach also works reciprocally. In principle, observed GW signals could be analyzed to constrain the Moon’s 3D internal structure \cite{2025arXiv250915452P}, complementing traditional seismic surveys. This interdependence hints at a promising future for lunar GW seismology as a dual‑purpose diagnostic tool.
